name: Acute Sinusitis (Rhinosinusitis)

veryLikely: Respiratory viruses (vast majority of acute sinusitis)
pathogens.why: Bacterial sinusitis is a secondary, less common event following viral URTI; criteria such as symptom duration >10 days or double-sickening identify the subset where bacterial superinfection by typical respiratory pathogens is likely enough to justify treatment.

investigations.why: Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is reserved for suspected complications (orbital/intracranial extension) or recurrent/chronic disease.

reason: Symptoms persisting beyond 10 days without improvement
, or a pattern of ‘double sickening’ (initial improvement followed by worsening)
, raise suspicion for bacterial superinfection of acute sinusitis. This meets criteria where a short course of antibiotics is reasonable, though many cases still resolve without them.

Symptoms of less than 10 days duration without double-sickening pattern are most consistent with viral rhinosinusitis. Antibiotics are not indicated at this stage; watchful waiting with symptomatic treatment is appropriate.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e pp. 296, 298-299 (Sinus Symptoms / Acute Sinusitis); orbital complications p. 276
clinicalPearls: The vast majority of acute sinusitis cases are caused by respiratory viruses; fewer than 2% of episodes are bacterial, yet antibiotics are prescribed at over 70% of office visits, making sinusitis a leading driver of unnecessary antibiotic use in adults (p. 299).
By guideline criteria, no more than about 50% of adults (and probably closer to 20%) with sinusitis actually meet thresholds for antibiotic prescribing (p. 299).
Symptoms are classified by duration: acute (<4 weeks), subacute (4-12 weeks), and chronic (>=12 weeks) (p. 298).

Common features are purulent nasal discharge, facial congestion/fullness, and facial pain or pressure; additional symptoms include fever, hyposmia or anosmia, ear pressure/pain, postnasal drip, halitosis, maxillary toothache, cough, and fatigue (p. 299).
Risk factors include age 45-65 years, smoking, asthma, air travel, and allergies (p. 299).
For an individual patient with a nonspecific upper respiratory illness, an antibiotic is more likely to cause an adverse reaction than to prevent a complication such as bacterial sinusitis (p. 296).
Recurrent acute sinusitis is defined as four or more episodes of acute sinusitis in a year with no signs or symptoms between episodes (p. 299).

Nosocomial sinusitis occurs in critically ill patients, often those who are nasotracheally intubated, and should be suspected in hospitalized patients with fever lacking another identifiable source (p. 299).
harrison.pathophysiology: Sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses; when the nasal passages are also involved the term rhinosinusitis is used. Most acute disease begins as a viral process. Bacterial sinusitis, when it occurs, is usually a secondary superinfection of the obstructed/inflamed sinus and is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, or M. catarrhalis. Invasive fungal disease arises when host defenses are impaired (uncontrolled diabetes, transplant/immunocompromise), allowing Mucorales or Aspergillus to invade tissue and spread beyond the sinus (pp. 298-299).
additionalDifferentials: Common cold / nonspecific upper respiratory infection (p. 298)
Rhinitis medicamentosa from overuse of topical decongestants (p. 298)
Drug-induced rhinitis (e.g., aspirin, ibuprofen, beta blockers) (p. 298)
Headache and facial pain syndromes referred to the sinuses (p. 298)
Gastroesophageal reflux causing referred sinus symptoms (p. 298)
infectionMimics: Bacterial superinfection masquerading within an otherwise viral course (p. 299)
Invasive fungal rhinosinusitis (Mucorales or Aspergillus) presenting as rapidly progressive sinusitis in immunocompromised hosts (p. 299)
Nosocomial sinusitis in intubated critically ill patients presenting as unexplained fever (p. 299)
nonInfectiousMimics: Autoimmune disease such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (p. 298)
Allergic rhinitis and other noninfectious rhinitides (p. 298)
Structural causes such as deviated nasal septum or nasal polyps (noted in chronic disease, p. 300)
additionalInvestigations: No imaging or laboratory testing is routinely required for uncomplicated acute sinusitis; diagnosis is clinical (pp. 299-300).
Sinus transillumination is NOT accurate for diagnosing sinusitis and should not be relied upon (p. 299).
Noncontrast CT is the preferred imaging modality when imaging is indicated (e.g., failure to improve, suspected complication, or alternative diagnosis) (p. 300).
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the preferred imaging modality when invasive fungal sinusitis is suspected (p. 299).
Nasal endoscopy with biopsy is part of the evaluation for suspected invasive fungal sinusitis (p. 299).
Direct rhinoscopy may reveal excess mucus or purulence on examination (p. 299).
In recurrent acute sinusitis, consider nasal culture during episodes, imaging between episodes to identify predisposing anatomic abnormalities, and allergic/immunologic evaluation (p. 300).
redFlags: Rapidly progressive facial pain/pressure with headache and fever in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient (suspect invasive fungal disease - an emergency) (p. 299)
Sinus symptoms that worsen after an initial improvement (double-sickening pattern) (p. 300)
Rapid worsening of facial pain that becomes persistent (p. 300)
harrison.prognosis: Most acute sinusitis is viral and self-limited. Symptoms of the underlying upper respiratory illness generally peak early but can persist up to about 14 days (p. 296). Complications of sinusitis can be dramatic but are extremely rare (p. 299). Invasive fungal sinusitis is an emergency: in immunocompromised hosts it can progress within days from rhinosinusitis to cranial nerve involvement, orbital and ophthalmic involvement, and critical illness (p. 299).
pitfalls: Treating acute sinusitis as bacterial by default - the large majority are viral, and antibiotics are over-prescribed; reserve antibiotics for patients meeting persistent (>=10 days), severe, or worsening criteria (p. 299).
Relying on sinus transillumination, which is inaccurate for diagnosis (p. 299).
Prescribing a macrolide for sinusitis - specifically not recommended because of high rates of macrolide-resistant S. pneumoniae (p. 300).
Missing invasive fungal sinusitis in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with rapidly progressive disease - delay can be fatal (p. 299).
Overlooking nosocomial sinusitis as a hidden source of unexplained fever in nasotracheally intubated ICU patients (p. 299).
In children, failing to consider a nasal foreign body as the cause of sinus symptoms (p. 298).
harrison.severityClassification: Antibiotic-prescribing indications (Harrison Table 37-2, p. 299): Persistent = symptoms lasting >=10 days; Severe = fever >102 degrees F with either purulent nasal discharge or nasal pain for at least 3-4 consecutive days; Worsening = new fever, headache, or increased nasal discharge following an upper respiratory infection that had lasted 5-6 days and was initially improving (double-sickening). Duration-based: acute <4 weeks, subacute 4-12 weeks, chronic >=12 weeks (p. 298).
